p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Maya and ___ went skiing at Copper Mountain."
e: The pronoun is part of the subject, so use the subject form. Test it alone: "I went skiing."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "The coach gave the trophy to Ava and ___."
e: After the word "to," use the object form. Test it alone: "The coach gave the trophy to me."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "___ and her brother built a snow fort."
e: The pronoun is part of the subject, so use the subject form: "She built a snow fort."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Between you and ___, the cat ate the cake."
e: "Between" is a preposition, so the pronouns after it use the object form: "between you and me."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "The dragon flew toward ___ and our friends."
e: After the preposition "toward," use the object form: "The dragon flew toward us."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "___ girls won the soccer tournament."
e: The pronoun goes with the subject "girls," so use the subject form. Drop "girls" to test it: "We won."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Mom made pancakes for ___ kids."
e: After the preposition "for," use the object form. Drop "kids" to test it: "Mom made pancakes for us."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Is this backpack ___?"
e: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun that can stand alone. "Your" needs a noun after it, like "your backpack."

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "The cat licked ___ paw."
e: "Its" shows ownership. "It's" means "it is," which does not fit here.

p: Which word in this sentence is a possessive pronoun? "The blue skis are hers."
e: "Hers" is a pronoun that shows ownership: the skis belong to her.

p: Which sentence uses pronouns correctly?
c: He and I went to the beach.
Him and me went to the beach.
He and me went to the beach.
Him and I went to the beach.
e: Both pronouns are part of the subject, so both need the subject form: "He went" and "I went."

p: Which sentence about the teacher uses pronouns correctly?
c: The teacher thanked Liam and me.
The teacher thanked Liam and I.
The teacher thanked Liam and myself.
The teacher thanked Liam and mine.
e: The pronoun receives the action of "thanked," so use the object form: "The teacher thanked me."

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "___ is knocking on the door?"
e: "Who" is the subject form. Here it does the knocking, so "who" is correct.

p: Which pronoun is in the object form (objective case)?
e: "Him" is the object form of "he." She, they, and we are subject forms.

p: Which pronoun is in the subject form (subjective case)?
e: "They" is a subject form. Them, us, and her are object forms.

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Our team and ___ will meet at the rink."
e: The pronoun is part of the subject, so use the subject form: "They will meet at the rink."

p: Which word in this sentence is an intensive pronoun? "The chef herself served the soup."
e: "Herself" adds emphasis to "chef." You could remove it and the sentence would still make sense.

p: Choose the intensive pronoun that completes the sentence: "We ___ painted the whole fence."
e: "Ourselves" matches "we" and adds emphasis.

p: What does an intensive pronoun do?
c: It adds emphasis to a noun or pronoun already named
It shows that something is a question
e: An intensive pronoun, like "myself" in "I myself saw it," adds emphasis. The sentence still works without it.

p: Which sentence uses an intensive pronoun?
e: In "I myself saw the bear," the word "myself" only adds emphasis. In "I hurt myself," it is a reflexive pronoun because it receives the action.

p: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun, not an intensive one?
c: The mayor herself opened the park.
e: In "The cat cleaned itself," the pronoun receives the action and cannot be removed. The others only add emphasis.

p: Choose the correct word: "The boys built the raft by ___."
e: "Themselves" is the standard form. "Theirselves" is not standard English.

p: Choose the intensive pronoun that completes the sentence: "He ___ climbed Pikes Peak."
e: "Himself" matches "he." "Hisself" is not standard English.

p: Which of these is a standard English word?
e: "Yourselves" is standard. The standard forms of the others are himself, themselves, and ourselves.

p: Which sentence has an incorrect shift in pronoun person?
c: When a skier falls, you should get up slowly.
When you ski, you should wear a helmet.
When skiers fall, they should get up slowly.
When I ski, I wear a helmet.
e: The sentence starts with "a skier" (third person) and switches to "you" (second person).

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "The two girls brought ___ own water bottles."
e: "The two girls" is plural, so the pronoun must be plural: "their."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "If students want to join, ___ should sign up today."
e: "Students" is plural and in the third person, so use "they."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "The dragons spread ___ wings."
e: "Dragons" is plural, so use the plural pronoun "their."

p: In the sentence "Students should bring your pencils," which word should replace "your"?
e: "Students" is plural and in the third person, so "their" matches it. "Your" is a shift to the second person.

p: What is wrong with this sentence? "We went to the beach, and you could see dolphins everywhere."
e: The sentence starts with "we" and switches to "you." A better version: "We went to the beach, and we could see dolphins everywhere."

p: Which sentence has a vague pronoun?
c: When Mia called Zoe, she was at the rink.
Mia called Zoe from the rink.
Mia was at the rink and called Zoe.
Zoe got a call from Mia at the rink.
e: In "When Mia called Zoe, she was at the rink," the word "she" could mean Mia or Zoe, so the reader cannot tell who was at the rink.

p: Why is this sentence unclear? "Ben told Sam that his skis were broken."
c: We cannot tell whose skis "his" means
e: "His" could mean Ben or Sam. That is a vague pronoun.

p: What makes "They" vague in this sentence? "They say it will snow tomorrow."
c: It does not say who "they" are
e: A pronoun should point to a clear noun. Here we do not know who "they" are. A clearer version: "The forecasters say it will snow tomorrow."

p: Which revision fixes the vague pronoun in "Take the cat out of the box and wash it"?
c: Take the cat out of the box and wash the box.
Take it out and wash it.
Take the cat out of it and wash it.
Take them out and wash it.
e: In the original, "it" could mean the cat or the box. Naming "the box" makes it clear.

p: Which sentence is clear about who ran?
c: When the dog saw the cat, the dog ran.
When the dog saw the cat, it ran.
The dog and the cat saw it, and it ran.
e: Naming "the dog" again removes the doubt. In "it ran," the reader cannot tell which animal ran.

p: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
c: Denver, the capital of Colorado, is called the Mile High City.
Denver the capital of Colorado, is called the Mile High City.
Denver, the capital of Colorado is called the Mile High City.
Denver the capital, of Colorado is called the Mile High City.
e: "The capital of Colorado" is extra information about Denver, so a pair of commas sets it off.

p: Which sentence uses parentheses correctly?
c: The Rocky Mountains (which run through Colorado) are huge.
The Rocky (Mountains which run through Colorado) are huge.
The Rocky Mountains (which run through) Colorado are huge.
(The Rocky Mountains which run) through Colorado are huge.
e: Parentheses go around the whole extra part: "which run through Colorado."

p: Which sentence uses a pair of dashes correctly?
c: My aunt—a ski instructor—taught me to carve turns.
My aunt a—ski instructor—taught me to carve turns.
My—aunt a ski instructor taught—me to carve turns.
My aunt a ski—instructor taught me—to carve turns.
e: The dashes go around the extra information "a ski instructor."

p: Commas, parentheses, and dashes can all be used to set off what?
c: Extra information that is not needed for the main meaning
The last word of a sentence
e: These marks set off extra (nonrestrictive) information. The sentence still makes sense without it.

p: Which sentence needs commas to set off extra information?
c: Mrs. Lopez our soccer coach loves pizza.
The girl who scored the goal is my sister.
e: "Our soccer coach" is extra information about Mrs. Lopez, so it needs commas: "Mrs. Lopez, our soccer coach, loves pizza."

p: Why are the commas used in this sentence? "Pikes Peak, a famous mountain, is near Colorado Springs."
c: They set off extra information about Pikes Peak
They separate items in a list
They show that someone is speaking
e: "A famous mountain" adds extra information about Pikes Peak, so commas set it off.

p: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
c: My brother, who is sixteen, just got his license.
My brother who is sixteen, just got his license.
My brother, who is sixteen just got his license.
My, brother who is sixteen just got his license.
e: Extra information in the middle of a sentence needs a comma on both sides.

p: Which sentence uses dashes correctly?
c: The beach my favorite—place was crowded—.
e: The dashes go around the extra information "my favorite place."

p: Which sentence about the dog is punctuated correctly?
c: Our dog, a golden retriever, loves the lake.
Our dog a golden retriever, loves the lake.
Our dog, a golden retriever loves the lake.
Our, dog a golden retriever loves the lake.
e: "A golden retriever" is extra information about the dog, so it needs a comma on both sides.

p: Which sentence about the soccer game uses parentheses correctly?
c: The soccer game (our last of the season) ended in a tie.
The soccer (game our last of the season) ended in a tie.
The soccer game (our last of the) season ended in a tie.
The (soccer game our last) of the season ended in a tie.
e: The parentheses go around the whole extra part: "our last of the season."

p: What does the Greek root "graph" (as in autograph) mean?
e: "Graph" means write. An autograph is a name you write yourself.

p: What does the Latin root "aud" (as in audience) mean?
e: "Aud" means hear. An audience listens, and audio is sound you hear.

p: What does the Latin root "port" (as in transport) mean?
e: "Port" means carry. To transport something is to carry it across a distance.

p: What does the Greek root "tele" (as in telescope) mean?
e: "Tele" means far. A telescope helps you see things that are far away.

p: What does the Latin root "rupt" (as in erupt) mean?
e: "Rupt" means break. When a volcano erupts, it breaks out.

p: What does the prefix "pre-" in "preview" mean?
e: "Pre-" means before. A preview is a look before the real thing.

p: What does the prefix "un-" in "unhappy" mean?
e: "Un-" means not. Unhappy means not happy.

p: What does the suffix "-less" in "fearless" mean?
e: "-less" means without. Fearless means without fear.

p: What does the Greek root "bio" (as in biology) mean?
e: "Bio" means life. Biology is the study of living things.

p: What does the Latin root "spect" (as in inspect) mean?
e: "Spect" means look. To inspect something is to look at it closely.

p: What kind of figurative language is this? "The snow was a white blanket over the town."
e: It compares snow to a blanket without using "like" or "as," so it is a metaphor.

p: What kind of figurative language is this? "Her smile was as bright as the sun."
e: It compares two things using "as," so it is a simile.

p: What kind of figurative language is this? "The stars danced in the night sky."
e: Stars cannot really dance. Giving a human action to a thing is personification.

p: What kind of figurative language is this? "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse."
e: It is a huge exaggeration for effect, which is called hyperbole.

p: Which word is an example of onomatopoeia?
e: Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like what it means. "Buzz" sounds like a bee.

p: What does "on fire" mean in this sentence? "Our team was on fire in the second half."
e: "On fire" is a figure of speech here. It means the team was playing very well.

p: Which word gives the most positive feeling about someone who is careful with money?
e: "Thrifty" has a positive connotation (feeling). Stingy, cheap, and greedy sound negative.

p: Which word has a negative connotation (feeling)?
e: "Nosy" means too interested in other people's business, which sounds negative. The others sound positive.

p: Complete the word relationship: Puppy is to dog as kitten is to ___.
e: A puppy is a young dog, so a kitten is a young cat.

p: Complete the word relationship: Hot is to cold as tall is to ___.
e: Hot and cold are opposites, so the answer is the opposite of tall: short.

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Grandpa took Leo and ___ fishing at Chatfield Lake."
e: The pronoun receives the action of "took," so use the object form. Test it alone: "Grandpa took me fishing."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Please save seats for my sister and ___."
e: After the preposition "for," use the object form. Test it alone: "Please save a seat for me."

p: Which sentence about the snowball fight uses pronouns correctly?
c: Jake threw a snowball at Ella and her.
Jake threw a snowball at Ella and she.
Jake threw a snowball at she and Ella.
Jake threw a snowball at Ella and herself.
e: After the preposition "at," use the object form "her." Test it alone: "Jake threw a snowball at her."

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "The dragon gave Rosa and ___ a shiny gold coin."
e: The pronoun receives the coin, so use the object form. Test it alone: "The dragon gave him a coin."

p: Choose the intensive pronoun that completes the sentence: "The twins ___ baked the birthday cake."
e: "The twins" is plural, so the matching intensive pronoun is "themselves." "Theirselves" is not standard English.

p: Which sentence uses "itself" as an intensive pronoun?
c: The castle itself was made of ice.
The robot taught itself to dance.
e: In "The castle itself was made of ice," the word "itself" only adds emphasis. You can remove it and the sentence still works.

p: Choose the intensive pronoun that completes the sentence: "I painted this dragon mural ___."
e: "Myself" matches "I" and adds emphasis: I did it with no help.

p: Which sentence keeps the same pronoun person all the way through?
c: When we hike, we bring plenty of water.
When we hike, you need plenty of water.
When I hike, you get thirsty fast.
When hikers climb, you should rest often.
e: "When we hike, we bring plenty of water" uses "we" both times. The others switch to "you" partway through.

p: Choose the pronoun that completes the sentence: "Lily and Grace packed ___ ski boots in the car."
e: "Lily and Grace" is two people, so use the plural pronoun "their."

p: Which word should replace "you" to fix the shift in this sentence? "Snowboarders know that you must wax the board often."
e: "Snowboarders" is plural and in the third person, so "they" matches it.

p: Choose the pronoun that keeps the sentence consistent: "When my friends and I go sledding, ___ always race to the bottom."
e: "My friends and I" means the same group as "we," so the pronoun stays in the first person.

p: Which sentence about the new snowboard has a vague pronoun?
c: Dad told Uncle Sam that he needed a new snowboard.
Dad told Uncle Sam, "I need a new snowboard."
Dad needed a new snowboard, so he told Uncle Sam.
Uncle Sam heard that Dad needed a new snowboard.
e: In "Dad told Uncle Sam that he needed a new snowboard," the word "he" could mean Dad or Uncle Sam, so the reader cannot tell who needs the snowboard.

p: Which revision fixes the vague pronoun in "The ball hit the window, and it broke"?
c: The ball hit the window, and the window broke.
The ball hit the window, and it was broken.
It hit the window, and it broke.
e: In the original, "it" could mean the ball or the window. Naming "the window" makes it clear.

p: Why is "it" vague in this sentence? "I put my phone on the sled, and then it slid down the hill."
c: "It" could mean the phone or the sled
e: Two things come before "it," so the reader cannot tell which one slid down the hill.

p: Which sentence about snacks uses standard English?
e: Standard English uses one negative word, not two. "Don't have any" is correct.

p: Which sentence about the soccer game uses standard English?
c: We should have won the game.
We should of won the game.
We should've of won the game.
e: The correct phrase is "should have." "Should of" comes from how "should've" sounds, but it is not standard.

p: Which sentence about the race uses standard English?
c: Marco ran really well in the race.
Marco ran real good in the race.
Marco ran good in the race.
Marco ran real well in the race.
e: "Well" and "really" are adverbs, which describe how he ran. "Good" and "real" are adjectives.

p: Which sentence about Mesa Verde uses commas correctly?
c: Mesa Verde, a national park in Colorado, has ancient cliff dwellings.
Mesa Verde a national park in Colorado, has ancient cliff dwellings.
Mesa Verde, a national park in Colorado has ancient cliff dwellings.
Mesa Verde, a national park, in Colorado has ancient cliff dwellings.
e: "A national park in Colorado" is extra information about Mesa Verde, so it needs a comma on both sides.

p: Which sentence about lunch uses dashes correctly?
c: Lunch—tacos and corn—was the best part of the field trip.
Lunch tacos—and corn—was the best part of the field trip.
Lunch—tacos and corn was—the best part of the field trip.
Lunch tacos and—corn was the best—part of the field trip.
e: The dashes go around the extra information "tacos and corn."

p: Which sentence about the cat uses parentheses correctly?
c: My cat Biscuit (who is afraid of mice) hides under the bed.
My cat (Biscuit who is afraid) of mice hides under the bed.
My cat Biscuit (who is afraid of mice hides) under the bed.
My (cat Biscuit who is) afraid of mice hides under the bed.
e: The parentheses go around the whole extra part: "who is afraid of mice."

p: Which sentence needs a pair of commas around extra information?
c: Coach Kim our ski instructor waved from the lift.
The skier who fell first got up quickly.
e: "Our ski instructor" is extra information about Coach Kim: "Coach Kim, our ski instructor, waved from the lift." In "The skier who fell first got up quickly," the words "who fell first" tell which skier, so it needs no commas.

p: Which word is spelled correctly?
e: "Necessary" has one c and two s's.

p: Choose the correctly spelled word: "We had a ___ time at the beach."
e: The suffix "-ful" has only one l.

p: Which of these words is spelled correctly?
e: "Beautiful" is spelled b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l, with one l at the end.

p: Choose the correctly spelled word: "Our soccer team hopes to ___ the trophy next year."
e: Remember the rule: "i before e, except after c." So it is "receive."

p: Which word is misspelled?
e: The correct spelling is "tomorrow," with one m and two r's.

p: Which choice combines these sentences best? "The dragon was huge. The dragon was green. The dragon slept in a cave."
c: The huge green dragon slept in a cave.
The dragon was huge, the dragon was green, the dragon slept in a cave.
The dragon was huge and the dragon was green and it slept in a cave.
Huge. Green. The dragon slept in a cave.
e: Moving "huge" and "green" in front of "dragon" makes one smooth sentence without repeating words.

p: Which sentence begins with a prepositional phrase?
c: Under the bridge, a troll counted his coins.
A troll counted his coins under the bridge.
e: "Under the bridge" is a prepositional phrase, and it starts the sentence. Starting this way is one way to vary sentence patterns.

p: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
c: It snowed all night, and the schools closed.
When it snowed all night, the schools closed.
The snow and the wind kept us inside.
e: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences with a comma and a word like "and," "but," or "so."

p: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
c: Because the lift was closed, we hiked up the hill.
The lift was closed, so we hiked up the hill.
We and our friends hiked up the hill.
e: A complex sentence has a part that cannot stand alone, like "Because the lift was closed," joined to a complete sentence.

p: Which sentence fits best in a formal science report?
c: The water boiled at 212 degrees Fahrenheit.
The water got super hot and boiled, lol.
OMG, the water boiled so fast!
Dude, the water was like totally boiling.
e: A formal report uses clear facts and no slang.

p: Which sentence keeps the formal tone of this report? "The museum displays fossils found in western Colorado."
c: Many of the fossils are more than 100 million years old.
Those bones are, like, crazy old!
e: "Many of the fossils are more than 100 million years old" states a fact in a calm, formal way. The others use slang and do not match.

p: Which closing fits best in a letter to the mayor asking for a new skate park?
c: Thank you for considering this request.
e: A letter to the mayor should sound polite and formal.

p: Use context clues: "The trail was so steep and rocky that only the most intrepid hikers dared to climb it." What does "intrepid" mean?
e: "Dared to climb" a steep, rocky trail is a clue that intrepid hikers are brave.

p: Use context clues: "After running the marathon, Dad was famished and ate three plates of pasta." What does "famished" mean?
e: Eating three plates of pasta is a clue that Dad was very hungry.

p: Use context clues: "The kitten was timid; it hid under the couch whenever guests came over." What does "timid" mean?
e: Hiding from guests is a clue that the kitten is shy.

p: Use context clues: "Unlike his gregarious sister, who loved parties, Theo preferred to read alone." What does "gregarious" mean?
e: "Unlike" signals a contrast with Theo, who likes to be alone. His sister loves parties, so she is outgoing.

p: Use context clues: "The beach was pristine, with no trash or footprints anywhere in the sand." What does "pristine" mean?
e: "No trash or footprints" is a clue that the beach was clean and untouched.

p: Use context clues: "The coach told us to conserve our energy, so we walked instead of running during warm-ups." What does "conserve" mean?
e: Walking instead of running is a way to save energy.

p: What does the Latin root "dict" (as in predict) mean?
e: "Dict" means say. To predict is to say what will happen before it happens.

p: What does the Greek root "phon" (as in telephone) mean?
e: "Phon" means sound. A telephone carries sound from far away.

p: What does the Latin root "scrib" or "script" (as in describe) mean?
e: "Scrib" and "script" mean write. A manuscript is something written by hand.

p: What does the prefix "re-" in "rewrite" mean?
e: "Re-" means again. To rewrite is to write again.

p: What does the suffix "-ful" in "joyful" mean?
e: "-ful" means full of. Joyful means full of joy.

p: What does the Greek root "geo" (as in geography) mean?
e: "Geo" means earth. Geography is the study of the earth's land and places.

p: Which reference book would best help you find a synonym for "happy"?
e: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings (synonyms). An atlas has maps, and an almanac has yearly facts.

p: A dictionary entry shows "can·yon." What do the dots show?
c: where the word breaks into syllables
how many letters the word has
e: Dictionaries use dots to split a word into syllables: can-yon.

p: Which word would come first in alphabetical order in a dictionary?
e: All four start with "bl." Then "i" comes before "o" and "u," and "blin" comes before "bliz" because "n" comes before "z."

p: What does this personification mean? "The old car groaned up the mountain road."
c: The car made loud, straining noises as it climbed
e: Cars cannot really groan. The writer means the car made tired, heavy sounds as it climbed.

p: Which sentence uses personification?
c: The wind whispered through the aspen trees.
The wind was as strong as a bull.
e: Wind cannot really whisper. Giving it a human action is personification. "As strong as a bull" is a simile.

p: What does the idiom "break the ice" mean in this sentence? "At the new school, Ana told a joke to break the ice."
e: To "break the ice" means to help people feel comfortable when they first meet.

p: What does "a piece of cake" mean in this sentence? "The spelling test was a piece of cake."
e: "A piece of cake" is an idiom that means something was very easy.

p: Complete the word relationship: Finger is to hand as toe is to ___.
e: A finger is part of a hand, and a toe is part of a foot. This is a part-to-whole relationship.

p: What is the relationship between "wheel" and "bicycle"?
e: A wheel is one part of a whole bicycle.

p: What is the relationship between "heavy rain" and "flood"?
e: Heavy rain can cause a flood. The rain is the cause, and the flood is the effect.

p: Complete the word relationship: Bird is to nest as bear is to ___.
e: A nest is a bird's home, and a den is a bear's home.

p: Which pair shows the same relationship as "chapter : book"?
e: A chapter is part of a book, and a player is part of a team. Both are part-to-whole.

p: Which word has the most positive connotation for someone who does not give up?
e: "Determined" sounds positive. "Stubborn" and "pigheaded" describe the same trait in a negative way.

p: Which word for a thin person has the most negative connotation?
e: "Scrawny" suggests too thin and weak. Slim, slender, and lean sound positive.

p: Which word gives the most positive feeling about a small house?
e: "Cozy" makes a small space sound warm and comfortable. "Cramped" and "crowded" sound negative.

p: Which word for a smell has a positive connotation?
e: "Fragrance" means a pleasant smell. The others suggest a bad smell.

p: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: "The box of crayons ___ on the table."
e: The subject is "box," which is singular. "Of crayons" does not change it, so use "is."

p: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: "Neither the cat nor the dogs ___ hungry."
e: With "neither...nor," the verb matches the closer subject. "Dogs" is plural, so use "are."

p: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: "Each of the skiers ___ a helmet."
e: "Each" is singular, so it takes the singular verb "wears."

p: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: "My friends and I ___ to the beach every summer."
e: "My friends and I" is a plural subject, so use the plural verb "go."

p: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
c: The dragons in the cave guard the gold.
The dragons in the cave guards the gold.
The dragon in the cave guard the gold.
The dragons in the cave is guarding the gold.
e: The plural subject "dragons" needs the plural verb "guard."

p: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
c: The puppy with the red collar.
e: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.

p: Which choice is a run-on sentence?
c: We went skiing we had fun.
We went skiing, and we had fun.
We went skiing. We had fun.
We went skiing; we had fun.
e: "We went skiing we had fun" joins two sentences with no punctuation or joining word.

p: Which choice correctly fixes this run-on? "The game was tied the crowd went wild."
c: The game was tied, and the crowd went wild.
The game was tied, the crowd went wild.
The game was tied and, the crowd went wild.
The game, was tied the crowd went wild.
e: A comma plus "and" correctly joins two complete sentences. A comma alone is not enough.

p: Why is "When the snow finally melted." not a complete sentence?
c: It does not express a complete thought
e: It has a subject (snow) and a verb (melted), but "When" leaves us waiting to learn what happened.

p: Which choice fixes this fragment? "Because the lift was closed."
c: Because the lift was closed, we went home.
Because the lift was closed and.
The lift. Because it was closed.
e: Adding a complete sentence, "we went home," finishes the thought.

p: Which phrase correctly shows that one dog owns a bone?
e: For one owner, add an apostrophe and s: "dog's."

p: Which phrase correctly shows the jerseys that belong to several players?
e: For a plural noun that ends in s, add only an apostrophe: "players'."

p: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
e: "Cat's" shows that the whiskers belong to the cat. Do not use an apostrophe to make a word plural.

p: Which phrase correctly shows the toys that belong to the children?
e: "Children" is already plural and does not end in s, so add an apostrophe and s: "children's."

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "___ going to the rodeo on Saturday."
e: "They're" means "they are": "They are going to the rodeo."

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "___ snowing again in the mountains."
e: "It's" means "it is": "It is snowing again."

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "The loud music had a big ___ on the dragon's mood."
e: "Effect" is usually a noun that means a result. Here it follows "a big," so it is a noun.

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "Lack of sleep can ___ how well you play soccer."
e: "Affect" is usually a verb that means to change or influence something.

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "My cat is bigger ___ your cat."
e: "Than" is used to compare. "Then" tells about time.

p: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "Are you going ___ the beach?"
e: "To" shows direction. "Too" means also or very, and "two" is the number 2.

p: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
c: We visited Rocky Mountain National Park in July.
We visited rocky mountain national park in July.
We visited Rocky Mountain National Park in july.
we visited Rocky Mountain National Park in July.
e: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, names of places, and months.

p: Which word in this sentence should be capitalized? "Last summer my family drove to aspen."
e: Aspen is the name of a town, so it is a proper noun. Seasons like summer are not capitalized.

p: Which sentence about the holiday uses capital letters correctly?
c: On Thanksgiving, Grandma made pumpkin pie.
On thanksgiving, Grandma made pumpkin pie.
On Thanksgiving, grandma made Pumpkin Pie.
on Thanksgiving, Grandma made pumpkin pie.
e: Holidays are capitalized. "Grandma" is used as a name here, so it is capitalized too. "Pumpkin pie" is a common noun.

p: Which end mark should finish this sentence? "Did you see the shooting star"
e: The sentence asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.

p: Which question about the soccer ball is punctuated correctly?
e: A question ends with a question mark, and no comma belongs after "Where."

p: Which word in this sentence is an adverb? "The fox quickly ran across the snowy field."
e: "Quickly" tells how the fox ran, so it is an adverb.

p: Which word in this sentence is an adjective? "The sleepy dragon yawned."
e: "Sleepy" describes the dragon, so it is an adjective.

p: Which word in this sentence is a verb? "Our goalie blocked the shot."
e: "Blocked" is the action the goalie did, so it is a verb.

p: Which word in this sentence is a preposition? "The cat hid under the porch."
e: "Under" shows where the cat is in relation to the porch, so it is a preposition.
